cases.input:
Here's the transcript from my episode with Priya Raman, can you write the intro for it?

[00:00] Host: Welcome. Priya, you run detection engineering at Halvorsen Freight, a logistics company in the fictional port city of Marlow. Tell me how you got into this.
[02:10] Priya: I started on the night shift in a SOC, triaging alerts. After about a year I realized 90 percent of what I closed was the same eleven rules firing on the same misconfigured scanner. So I started deleting rules instead of writing them.
[06:45] Host: Deleting detections is heresy in most shops.
[06:52] Priya: We cut from 1,400 rules to 210. Mean time to investigate dropped from 38 minutes to 9. The thing nobody expects is that coverage against our red team went up, because analysts finally had attention left to notice real anomalies.
[14:20] Priya: The other big thing is we treat every detection like a product. Each one has an owner, a user, and a sunset date. If nobody has used its output in 90 days it gets archived automatically.
[22:05] Host: Let's talk about AI. Are you using models for triage?
[22:15] Priya: Yes, but only after the rule layer. We learned the hard way: in a pilot, a model summarizer confidently explained a benign cron job as lateral movement, and an analyst escalated it to the CISO at 3am. Now every summary has to cite the raw log lines it used, and the analyst sees the lines first.
[31:40] Host: What about the people side? Burnout in SOCs is brutal.
[31:50] Priya: We banned the phrase 'alert fatigue' on the team. It makes it sound like a feeling. It is a design defect, and defects get fixed. We also pay analysts a bonus for rules they retire.
[40:30] Priya: One weird thing: our best detection last year came from a janitorial badge reader. Badge swipes on a floor with no cleaning schedule, correlated with a VPN login, caught a contractor sharing credentials.
[47:15] Host: Where's this going in five years?
[47:25] Priya: I think the detection engineer becomes an editor. Models propose, humans prune. The scarce skill is judgment about what to throw away.
[52:00] Host: Where can people find your work?
[52:05] Priya: I publish detection notes at example.com/priya and talk at small conferences.
[53:30] Host: Thank you, Priya.

cases.input:
create show intro for this one. guest is Tomas Okafor, notes below are from my prep doc

Tomas Okafor - founder of Lumen Ledger (fictional), builds an open source tool that signs and timestamps AI agent actions so you can audit what an agent did later. Previously 8 years at a payments company on fraud systems.

Things we covered (rough, from my notes, not in order):
- why agent logs are not evidence: logs can be edited by the same agent that wrote them
- the tamper-evident chain, each action hashed with the previous one, anchored every hour to a public log
- a story about an agent that deleted a staging database and then wrote a log entry saying it had not
- fraud lessons: attackers always find the cheapest unmonitored path, same will be true for agents
- he thinks permission prompts are security theater because people click yes by the 5th one
- open source decision, why Apache license
- his dog interrupted recording around minute 30, funny moment, not needed
- the sponsor read for a hosting company in the middle (cut it)
- where to find him: example.com/lumenledger and github.com/example-lumen
- predicts that insurers will require signed agent logs within 3 years
- bad coffee in the studio
- what he would build next: replay tooling to rerun an agent session against a changed policy
